howTheseWereProduced.keys: Ephemeral NIST P-256 key pairs generated once; the private halves were never written anywhere and no longer exist.
howTheseWereProduced.immutability: trust-registry/v1/ is immutable exactly like a released schema directory and commitment/v1/. ECDSA is randomized, so regenerating would produce different signatures; these are the published bytes and they are what both runtimes must agree on.
howTheseWereProduced.twoLayers: The deterministic material (thumbprints, canonical bytes, digests) must be reproduced byte for byte by any runtime. The signed material must be accepted or refused identically, with the same reason code.

canonical.note: The canonical JSON of registry version 1, i.e. the signing input with its NUL-separated header removed. Published in full as the readable anchor; every other manifest is pinned by its digest, and a digest match is a byte match.

keys.revocationReason: Suspected exposure of the signing identity during a support session.
Suspected exposure of the signing identity during a support session.
Key material assumed compromised from the stated time onward.
Labelled active while carrying a revocation date in the past.

chainCases.description: The published history, accepted in order: publish, rotate in, retire out, revoke late, revoke early.
A verifier with no state accepts the first manifest and remembers it.
Being handed the manifest already held is not an attack and not a change; the state does not move.
An older, still perfectly signed manifest. This is how a revocation is hidden, so it is refused rather than merely ignored.
Jumping a version would accept key history nobody checked, even though the manifest itself is valid.
Two different manifests at one registry version. Both verify; one version has one history, and no rule can pick the honest side.
Correctly signed, but its predecessor digest names a document this verifier never saw.
A complete, self-consistent registry issued by somebody else. A pinned verifier refuses it instead of offering to trust the new root.
One character of the issue time changed after the root signed it.
Verification with no anchor at all. Refused: it would trust whatever key history it was given.
The right root thumbprint under the wrong issuer name.

refusalCases.description: A published key entry carrying a private component. Node would build a working public key from it and nothing would look wrong.
A declared thumbprint that is not the thumbprint of the key beside it. The thumbprint is what a pin is taken over, so it is recomputed and never believed.
A key labelled ACTIVE while carrying a revocation date in the past. A reader who trusted the label would trust a revoked key.
A valid signature, made by a key whose published use is signing evidence. If it counted, whoever could seal a record could rewrite which keys are trusted.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: The ordinary case: an active key, the right record, the right content.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: No independently computed digest was supplied, so the content dimension is honestly unchecked and the verdict can never be the strongest one.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: The seal is signed correctly but commits to different content.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: The signing key has since been retired by an ordinary rotation. Historical verification is unaffected: the key was active when it signed.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: The key was later revoked, with the compromise back-dated to after this seal. Worth something, but the boundary is a time Pruvz asserted about itself.

sealCases.subject: s2
sealCases.description: The same key, the same kind of signature — but made after the declared compromise began. Flattening this and the case above into one boolean is exactly what time-aware output exists to prevent.

sealCases.subject: s2
sealCases.description: The successor key, verified while it was active.

sealCases.subject: s2
sealCases.description: A seal presented against an older registry that does not carry its key yet. Unknown is a refusal, never an assumption.

sealCases.subject: s2
sealCases.description: A perfectly valid signature about a different record. Validity and relevance are separate questions.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: One bit of the signature flipped.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: The profile is inside the signature, so raising a pre-customer seal to a customer-production one changes the bytes instead of changing what the signature is understood to mean.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: A genuine signature by the trust root. A root that could also seal evidence would let whoever controls key history mint records.

sealCases.subject: s1
sealCases.description: A key id the published history has never carried.
